mcq.q: Decode at small batch is usually limited by…
mcq.why: Each step reads all weights for little arithmetic, so bandwidth dominates.
distractors: Small batches do little maths per weight read.
Weights are already in GPU memory, not read from disk.
The network is not on the per-token path.

mcq.q: Why is prefill compute-bound?
options: It waits for the network between each of the prompt tokens
All prompt tokens go in one pass, with lots of maths per weight read
It runs on the CPU, which is much slower at matrix maths
It reads the full weights once again for every prompt token
mcq.why: Many tokens share each weight read, so the GPU runs near its FLOP limit.
distractors: It reads them once for the whole prompt.

mcq.q: What makes up time to first token (TTFT)?
options: Network time to the server only
Decode time for the whole answer
mcq.why: TTFT grows with prompt length.
distractors: That comes after the first token.
That is the rest of the answer.

mcq.q: Using the figure's rates (prefill 10,000 tokens/s, decode 60 tokens/s), what is TTFT for a 20,000-token prompt with no queue?
End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × ITL. With TTFT 0.5 s, 301 output tokens and ITL 20 ms, what is it?
Long prompts mostly hurt ___; long outputs mostly hurt ___.
mcq.why: Prompts are prefilled before the first token; outputs are decoded after it.
distractors: ITL barely changes with prompt length.

mcq.q: Why does batching help decode throughput?
options: It makes each token cheaper to compute alone
Many sequences share each weight read
mcq.why: Decode is bandwidth-bound; batching amortises the read.

mcq.q: In the laptop lab, why is the second TTFT lower when you rerun the same prompt?
options: The model got smaller after loading
Decode ran faster the second time
Ollama reused the cached prompt prefix
The CPU warmed the disk cache for it
mcq.why: Prefix caching skips prefill for the repeated part (14.3).
distractors: Decode affects later tokens, not TTFT.

mcq.q: Why is dividing total tokens by total time a poor metric for a chat service?
options: It needs a GPU profiler to be computed
It hides whether the wait was before or during output
It always comes out close to zero for chat
It overstates the time to the first token
mcq.why: Users perceive TTFT and ITL separately.
distractors: It does not measure TTFT at all.

mcq.q: Which do chat users perceive most?
mcq.why: Chat users notice the wait before text appears; batch jobs care about total time.

mcq.q: A chat reply has TTFT of 0.3 s and an inter-token latency of 20 ms, and it is 200 tokens long. Roughly what is the end-to-end latency?
distractors: That is only the time to the first token.
That counts the decode tokens but leaves out TTFT.

distractors: That leaves out the queue wait.
That is only the queue wait.
That uses a decode rate of about 60 tokens/s for prefill.

mcq.q: What does paged attention mainly fix?
options: Model size on disk and in memory
mcq.why: Fixed-size blocks allocated on demand avoid reserving max-length contiguous memory.
distractors: Paging changes memory layout, not attention results.

mcq.q: What is the main problem with static batching?
options: It cannot run on GPUs, so batches must run on CPU servers
Short requests wait for the longest; newcomers wait for the batch
It uses too little GPU memory for the KV cache to be efficient
It changes the model's outputs for long and short requests alike
mcq.why: Slots sit idle while the longest request finishes.

mcq.q: What does continuous batching do?
options: Re-forms the batch each step: finished leave, waiting join
Runs one request at a time, strictly in order
Waits for N requests, then runs them together
Batches only the prefill step of each request
mcq.why: This typically multiplies throughput several-fold.

mcq.q: What is chunked prefill for?
options: Splitting a new prefill so decoding is not stalled
mcq.why: Long prefills are inserted in pieces between decode steps.

mcq.q: How does paged attention store the KV cache?
options: On disk, loaded block by block
In CPU memory only, for safety
In one max-length buffer per sequence
In fixed-size blocks, mapped by a block table
mcq.why: Like virtual memory pages; blocks can be shared.
distractors: That is the waste it removes.

mcq.q: A bot sends a 6,000-token shared prefix and 800 unique tokens per request. On a prefix-cache hit, how many tokens need prefill?
mcq.why: Only the unique part is prefilled on a hit.
distractors: That is the shared prefix, which is cached.
The unique part still needs prefill.

mcq.q: Input price $3 per million tokens, 90% cached-token discount. On a hit, what is the input cost of 6,000 cached plus 800 new tokens?
distractors: That leaves out the cached tokens.
That leaves out the new tokens.
That is a miss at full price.

mcq.q: How should prompts be structured to benefit from prefix caching?
options: Randomise the order on every call
It does not matter for caching
Stable content first; dynamic content after
mcq.why: The cache matches from the start of the prompt (7.2).
distractors: Changing the start breaks the shared prefix.

mcq.q: Does prefix caching reduce decode cost?
options: No: it skips part of prefill only
Yes, by the same factor as prefill
mcq.why: Decode still runs for every output token.
distractors: Decode still runs for every output token.

mcq.q: Is sharing prefix-cache blocks across tenants automatically safe?
options: Yes, caches are always safe to share between tenants
No: decide what may be shared; isolate tenant text
Only when the model is served by a hosted API
Yes, as long as every tenant uses the same model
mcq.why: Shared caches can leak information through timing or content if not designed carefully.
distractors: Shared blocks can expose tenant text.

mcq.q: Chat users see their streams pause whenever someone submits a long document, because its prefill blocks the decode steps of everyone else. Which engine feature addresses this?
options: Prefix caching of the long document for every user
Paged attention, which removes the cost of prefill
Chunked prefill, so the long prefill is split between decode steps
Static batching, so the document waits for the next batch
mcq.why: It inserts prefill in pieces so decoding continues.
distractors: Each document is new, so there is nothing cached.
Paging stores the KV cache; it does not shorten prefill.
That adds waiting and idle slots.

mcq.q: Why is self-hosting cost mostly fixed?
options: Electricity is free in data centres
You pay for GPU-hours, busy or idle
mcq.why: API cost is variable; self-hosting is fixed capacity.
distractors: They cost money whether busy or not.

mcq.q: Choose all the conditions under which self-hosting can win.
options: High, steady volume that keeps GPUs well used
A smaller open model meets the quality bar
mcq.why: Low, spiky traffic leaves GPUs idle.

mcq.q: 20 billion tokens a month at $0.60 per million via API costs…
One GPU at 2,500 tokens/s and 45% average utilisation delivers about how many tokens a month (about 2.63 million seconds)?
Where should the throughput input in the calculator come from?
options: A blog post about the model
Your own benchmark at your SLO
mcq.why: Vendor peaks overstate real throughput.

mcq.q: Which costs belong in a self-hosted total?
options: The model licence fee, which is the largest single cost
GPUs with redundancy, people, network, storage, monitoring, idle time
Electricity for the GPUs, at the data centre's rate
The GPU hourly price, multiplied by the GPU count
mcq.why: The full cost is much more than GPUs.

mcq.q: Harbor compares options by…
options: Dollars per resolved question at equal quality
The size of each candidate model
The number of GPUs each option needs
mcq.why: A cheap token is not cheap if the task needs many calls or human fixes.

mcq.q: Why is the calculator's minimum 2 GPUs?
mcq.why: One GPU is a single point of failure.

mcq.q: What is an opportunity cost of self-hosting?
mcq.why: Hosted providers ship new models you may not be able to run.

mcq.q: Tokens per GPU per month are 2.96 billion and demand is 20 billion. How many GPUs does the calculator use?
mcq.why: 20 / 2.96 ≈ 6.8, rounded up to 7 (above the minimum of 2).

mcq.q: Using the chapter's example figures (one GPU ≈ 2.96B tokens a month at 45% utilisation, about $1,830 per GPU-month, $15,000 a month of ops), compare self-hosting with an API at $0.60 per million tokens for 40B tokens a month.
options: 14 GPUs ≈ $40,600 against $24,000 for the API: the API is cheaper
14 GPUs ≈ $40,600 against $2,400: the API wins by far
distractors: That leaves out the $15,000 of ops.
